Arizona sun rule — work the seal before 11am, save the second coat for cooler air
🧭 On‑Site Field Guide

Sealing Kat's Roof Before It Bakes

A walk‑the‑perimeter guide to the cracks in the parapet cap — what they are, what to grab, and exactly what to do with the two hours you've got.

The Short Answer

Seal today. Topcoat once it's fully cured.

Every crack on this roof needs to be clean, filled, and sealed before anything else — that's the part that actually stops water getting in, and it's what your two hours are for. Painting is protection for the sealant, not the leak fix itself, so it can wait a day without any risk to the repair.

Today: clean → fill → seal → tool smooth. Tomorrow (or once tack‑free): topcoat with elastomeric roof coating.
Before You Climb

Four things to lock in first

It's Arizona heat on a roof — the deck and the cap will be hotter than the air. A little prep now keeps the two hours from turning into three.

🥾

Grippy, closed shoes

Painted stucco gets slick with dust. Skip anything with a smooth sole.

💧

Water within reach

Bring more than feels necessary. Sip on a timer, not just when thirsty.

🧤

Gloves + eye protection

Wire brushing old stucco throws grit — especially overhead near the coping edge.

📱

Someone knows you're up there

Quick text to Kat or a family member with a rough finish time. Costs nothing.

🪜

Ladder on solid, level ground

Re-check its footing before every climb — not just the first one.

⏱️

Start now, not at noon

Sealant skins over fast in direct heat — you want time to tool it before it sets.

What You're Looking At

Two crack types, two fixes

Walking the roofline, you'll see both of these. Telling them apart in the first thirty seconds decides which material you reach for.

Type A — Hairline

Surface cracks, paint‑deep

Thin, thread-like lines — you can just barely catch a fingernail in them. Mostly cosmetic paint film cracking from sun and thermal movement, but they're still an open door for water.

Fix: clean + one bead of elastomeric caulk, tooled flush. No backer needed.
Type B — Open / separation

Wider gaps, visible depth

You can see actual depth or exposed aggregate inside the crack, or it opens into a small void. These run through the stucco coating, not just the paint, so they move more with heat and need more material to bridge properly.

Fix: pack the void first (backer rod or elastomeric patch compound), then bridge with caulk — or embed mesh tape in the sealant for extra strength across the gap.
Kit List

What to grab before you climb

Prep

  • Wire brushLoosens old paint and crumbling stucco inside each crack.
  • Stiff dust brush or a can of compressed airSealant won't bond to dust — this step isn't optional.
  • Chalk or painter's tapeMark every crack as you find it on your first lap, so nothing gets missed on the second.
  • Utility knifeCuts back any loose, curling paint edges before filling.

Fill & Seal

  • Paintable elastomeric or polyurethane caulkLook for "elastomeric," "flexible," or "masonry" on the label — not standard acrylic.
  • Backer rod or elastomeric patch compoundFor the wider Type B gaps — fills depth so the caulk only bridges the surface.
  • Fiberglass or polyester mesh tapeOptional but worth having for any crack wider than a pencil lead.
  • Caulking gun + a damp rag or tooling stickFor smoothing each bead flush before it skins over.

Paint (today or on the return trip)

  • 100% acrylic elastomeric roof coatingNot regular wall paint — it needs to flex with the cap and block UV.
  • Angled brush + small rollerBrush the crack lines first, roll the field second.

Skip these

  • Pure silicone caulkNothing sticks to it afterward — paint will peel right off.
The Walkthrough

Step by step, in order

Do these in sequence — each step sets up the one after it.

1

Walk the whole perimeter first

10 min

Before touching anything, do one full lap of the roofline and mark every crack with chalk or tape. You already know they run the full length of the cap — find them all before you commit to a starting point, so you're not backtracking later in the heat.

2

Clean every marked crack

15–20 min

Wire-brush loose paint and crumbling stucco out of each crack, then blow or brush out the dust. Work the whole lap this way before you seal anything — it's faster in one pass than stopping to clean and seal one crack at a time.

A crack that isn't clean will just re-open under the new caulk within a season. This step is the one that's actually worth rushing least.
3

Pack the wide ones (Type B) first

10–15 min

This is the kind of gap that needs depth filled before it gets sealed over.

Press backer rod into any crack wider than a pencil lead, or trowel in elastomeric patch compound, so the crack's depth is filled and only a thin surface remains for the caulk to bridge. This keeps the caulk from sinking into the void later.

4

Run a bead over every crack

15–20 min

Load the caulking gun and run a continuous bead of elastomeric sealant over each crack — the hairline ones directly, the packed Type B ones as a bridge coat over the backer rod. For the widest spots, lay mesh tape into the wet bead and cover it with a second pass of caulk.

5

Tool every bead flush

5–10 min

Run a damp finger or tooling stick along each bead right after applying it, feathering the edges out onto the sound stucco on either side. This is what makes the repair invisible under paint later — don't skip it to save two minutes now.

6

Let it skin while you double-check the lap

30–45 min

In Arizona sun, most elastomeric sealants skin over (safe to touch, not yet fully cured) in 30–45 minutes. Use this window to walk the roof again and confirm you didn't miss a crack near a corner or drain — those spots hide easily on the first pass.

7

Topcoat — if it's skinned and you're in your window

15–20 min

Once a bead is dry to a light touch, brush elastomeric roof coating over it, feathering into the surrounding painted stucco. If a bead is still tacky when your two hours are up, leave it bare — it's already doing its job protecting the crack, and paint goes on fine tomorrow.

Decision Point

One trip or two?

Recommended

Seal today, paint on the next visit

Gives every bead a full cure — typically 24 hours in this heat — before it takes any UV or foot traffic. The crack is already sealed against water the moment you leave, so there's no risk in the wait.

If it has to be one trip

Seal early, topcoat late in the same visit

Works for the hairline (Type A) beads once they've skinned. For the deeper Type B repairs, a same-day topcoat over an uncured bead can trap moisture and crack later — better to leave those bare today and topcoat on a return trip.

Your Two Hours

A realistic breakdown

Adjust the minutes to how many cracks you actually count on the first lap, but this is roughly how it splits.

0:00 – 0:10

Setup & perimeter walk

Ladder, gear staged, every crack marked.

0:10 – 0:30

Clean the full lap

Brush and blow out every marked crack.

0:30 – 0:45

Pack the wide ones

Backer rod or patch compound into any Type B gap.

0:45 – 1:10

Seal & tool every crack

Caulk bead over all of them, mesh where needed, tooled flush.

1:10 – 1:45

Second lap while it skins

Recheck for missed spots; let the sealant firm up.

1:45 – 2:00

Topcoat what's ready, pack up

Brush coating over any bead that's dry to the touch; note what's left for next visit.

Worth Avoiding

Four ways to redo this next month

  • ✕
    Silicone caulk anywhere on this roofPaint won't bond to it — you'll be back here scraping it out later.
  • ✕
    Sealing over dust or loose paintThe bead looks fine going on and fails within weeks.
  • ✕
    Painting a bead that's still tacky underneathTraps moisture inside, and the paint film cracks again by next summer.
  • ✕
    Working straight through peak midday sunThe sealant skins before you can tool it smooth — start early, pause if you need to.
Keep an Eye On It

After today

Check the repaired spots after the first real rain, and again in six months. If the exact same spot reopens twice, that's a sign of ongoing structural movement in the cap rather than simple weathering — worth a roofer's opinion at that point, rather than a third round of caulk.
